parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The results of the $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment provide evidence for the structure of the atom.

Result 1: The vast majority of the $\alpha$-particles pass straight through the metal foil or are deviated by small angles.

Result 2: A very small minority of $\alpha$-particles is scattered through angles greater than $90^{\circ}$.

State what may be inferred (deduced) from:

markscheme_points.text: most of the atom is empty space or the nucleus (volume) is very small

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the alpha-particles must be travelling through if almost all of them miss everything and go straight on with no deflection.
parts.proper_answer: Most of the atom is empty space, so the nucleus occupies a very small volume.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what straight-through means**
Imagine firing tiny fast positive bullets at a thin foil. If nearly all go straight through untouched, they cannot be hitting much solid matter. You are seeing that atoms are mostly nothing.

Step 2: **Link to nuclear size**
The only thing that can deflect an alpha-particle strongly is the tiny central nucleus. Since hits are extremely rare, that nucleus must be very small compared with the whole atom. So result 1 tells you the atom is mostly empty space.

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: the mass is concentrated in nucleus or the majority of the mass is in nucleus

hints: Hint 1: Think about what kind of force could turn a fast, heavy, positively charged alpha-particle right back on itself through more than $90^{\circ}$.
Hint 2: Think about how heavy the object it hits must be if the light alpha-particle bounces back rather than pushing the object away.
parts.proper_answer: The nucleus is charged (positively charged) causing repulsion, and most of the atomic mass is concentrated in the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why a large-angle bounce needs charge**
An $\alpha$-particle has charge $+2e$. To repel it backwards you need a strong electrostatic repulsion. That means it has come very close to a small region of concentrated positive charge. So the nucleus must be charged.

Step 2: **Why a bounce needs large mass**
In a collision the lighter object bounces back. An $\alpha$-particle has mass about $4\text{ u}$. For it to be scattered back through $>90^{\circ}$, the object it hits must be much more massive than itself and must not recoil away easily. So almost all the mass of the atom must be concentrated in that tiny nucleus.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A radioactive decay sequence contains four nuclei, P, Q, R and S, as shown.

$$^{218}_{84}\text{P} \rightarrow ^{214}_{82}\text{Q} \rightarrow ^{214}_{83}\text{R} \rightarrow \text{S}$$

Nucleus S is an isotope of nucleus P.
parts.text: Determine the proton number and the nucleon number of nucleus S.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what the word isotope tells you about proton numbers, and compare nucleus S with nucleus P to fix one of the two numbers immediately.

Hint 2: Track how $A$ and $Z$ change in the first two steps, $^{218}_{84}\text{P} \rightarrow ^{214}_{82}\text{Q} \rightarrow ^{214}_{83}\text{R}$, to identify the decay types and then apply the same logic from R to S.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the isotope clue for the proton number**
Isotopes have the same proton number $Z$ with different nucleon number. Since S is an isotope of P, and P has $Z = 84$, then S must also have $$Z = 84$$

Step 2: **Read the decay chain to get the nucleon number**
From P to Q: $$A: 218 \rightarrow 214, \quad Z: 84 \rightarrow 82$$ This is $A-4$, $Z-2$, so an $\alpha$ decay. From Q to R: $$A: 214 \rightarrow 214, \quad Z: 82 \rightarrow 83$$ This is $A$ unchanged, $Z+1$, so a $\beta^-$ decay. From R to S, $Z$ must go $83 \rightarrow 84$ to reach the isotope value, which is again $Z+1$ with $A$ unchanged, so $$A = 214$$ Hence S is $^{214}_{84}\text{S}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The quark composition of a nucleon in Q changes as Q decays to form R.

Describe this change to the quark composition of the nucleon.

markscheme_points.text: up down down changes to up up down or down changes to up / $d \rightarrow u$

hints: Hint 1: Start from the $Z$ change in Q to R, $82 \rightarrow 83$ with $A$ unchanged, and remember which nucleon must change into which other nucleon for that to happen.
parts.proper_answer: A down quark changes to an up quark, $d \rightarrow u$, so a neutron ($udd$) becomes a proton ($uud$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the nucleon change**
Q to R keeps $A = 214$ but $Z$ increases by 1. That is the signature of $\beta^-$ decay, where a neutron turns into a proton inside the nucleus: $$n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$$

Step 2: **Write it in quarks**
A neutron is $udd$ and a proton is $uud$. So one down quark flips to up: $$udd \rightarrow uud$$ or simply $$d \rightarrow u$$
